title: Sunflowers
culture_origin: Dutch artist working in Arles, France
official_description: A yellow-on-yellow still life of fifteen sunflowers in different stages of growth and decay, painted in Arles.
historical_context: Van Gogh made the Arles sunflower paintings to decorate the Yellow House before Paul Gauguin's visit.
visual_description: Fifteen jagged, drooping, blooming, and seeding flowers fill a simple yellow vase against a pale yellow wall.

sources.title: Vincent van Gogh - Sunflowers - NG3863
sources.license_note: ATLAS paraphrase of the official museum record; no long museum text copied.

chunks.text: Vincent van Gogh painted this version of Sunflowers in Arles in 1888, using oil on canvas.
The National Gallery painting measures 92.1 by 73 centimetres, is signed Vincent, and has inventory number NG3863.
Van Gogh painted seven Arles versions in total during 1888 and 1889; five versions are now displayed in museums around the world.
He planned the paintings as decorations for the Yellow House before his friend and fellow artist Paul Gauguin arrived.
Van Gogh completed the first four sunflower canvases in one week, working quickly before the cut flowers faded.
This version shows fifteen sunflowers: some are buds, some are fully open, and others have lost petals and are turning to seed.
Thick impasto creates raised texture. Long strokes follow petals and stems, while small dabs imitate the rough seed heads.
Van Gogh limited the picture mainly to yellow, ranging from orange ochre to the pale greenish yellow of the background.
The vase is divided into two yellow bands, and Van Gogh signed his first name Vincent in blue on its left side.
The flowers' movement from bud to decay connects the still life with the vanitas tradition, which reflects on the temporary nature of life.
The National Gallery notes possible meanings of friendship, gratitude, and the beauty and vitality of nature.
Van Gogh painted fifteen bright sunflowers in one vase. Some are young, some are open, and some are becoming seeds, so we see the flowers changing over time.
The series was made in two groups: four canvases in August 1888 and three repetitions in January 1889, intended partly as companions to portraits of Madame Roulin.
The restricted yellow palette, calligraphic contours, directional strokes, and dense impasto make the still life an early statement of Van Gogh's mature Arles style.
Vincent van Gogh a peint cette version des Tournesols a Arles en 1888, a l'huile sur toile.
Van Gogh a peint sept versions a Arles en 1888 et 1889. Cinq sont aujourd'hui exposees dans des musees.
Il voulait decorer la Maison jaune avant l'arrivee de son ami et collegue Paul Gauguin.
Le vase contient quinze tournesols: des boutons, des fleurs ouvertes et des tetes qui perdent leurs petales et produisent des graines.
L'impasto epais cree du relief. Les longs traits suivent les petales et les tiges, tandis que de petites touches imitent les graines.
La palette est presque entierement jaune, de l'ocre orange au jaune pale legerement vert du fond.
Les etapes de la vie des fleurs rappellent la tradition des vanites. Elles peuvent aussi evoquer l'amitie, la gratitude et la vitalite de la nature.
Les sept Tournesols d'Arles ont ete realises en deux groupes: quatre tableaux en aout 1888, puis trois repetitions en janvier 1889.
Le tableau de Londres montre quinze tournesols et porte la signature Vincent sur le vase. C'est l'une des cinq versions exposees dans des musees.
